The wave is \( y = A\sin(Bx + Ct) \) with \( A, B, C \) all positive.

A particular point on the waveform is a point of CONSTANT PHASE, so
\( Bx + Ct = \) constant.

Differentiating with respect to \( t \):
\( B\dfrac{dx}{dt} + C = 0 \qquad \therefore \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -\dfrac{C}{B} \)

Since \( B \) and \( C \) are positive, \( \dfrac{dx}{dt} \) is NEGATIVE: as \( t \) increases, \( x \) must decrease to keep the phase the same.

\( \therefore \) the wave is travelling along the NEGATIVE \( x \)-direction, with speed \( v = \dfrac{C}{B} \).

The general rule: a phase of the form \( (kx - \omega t) \) means travel along \( +x \), while \( (kx + \omega t) \) — the two terms carrying the SAME sign, as here — means travel along \( -x \).

A point can be touched without disturbing the motion only if it is a NODE, because a node is permanently at rest. So the question is: where are the nodes in each mode of a string of length \( l \) fixed at both ends?

**Fundamental mode (first harmonic):** \( l = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \). The only nodes are the two fixed ends, with a single antinode at the centre.
\( \therefore \) apart from the two ends there is NO other position that can be touched. Touching anywhere else would damp the vibration.

**First overtone (second harmonic):** \( l = \lambda \), so there is one extra node midway between the ends.
\( \therefore \) the string can be touched at its MIDPOINT, i.e. at \( \dfrac{l}{2} \).

**Second overtone (third harmonic):** \( l = \dfrac{3\lambda}{2} \), so there are two extra nodes.
\( \therefore \) the string can be touched at \( \dfrac{l}{3} \) and at \( \dfrac{2l}{3} \) from either end.

| mode | \( l \) in terms of \( \lambda \) | nodes apart from the ends |
|---|---|---|
| fundamental | \( \lambda/2 \) | none |
| first overtone | \( \lambda \) | \( l/2 \) |
| second overtone | \( 3\lambda/2 \) | \( l/3 \) and \( 2l/3 \) |

When a string or an air column is set into vibration, waves reflected from the ends form stationary waves. The boundary conditions allow only certain wavelengths, and hence only certain frequencies, called the NATURAL FREQUENCIES or normal modes of the system.

**Fundamental frequency:** the minimum of these natural frequencies. The corresponding mode is the fundamental mode or fundamental tone. It is also called the FIRST HARMONIC.

**Harmonics:** the term harmonic is used when the frequency of a mode is an INTEGRAL MULTIPLE of the fundamental frequency. If the fundamental is \( n \), the harmonics are \( n, 2n, 3n, 4n, \ldots \); the \( p \)-th harmonic has frequency \( pn \). Harmonics form a complete arithmetic set defined by the fundamental — but all of them may not actually be present in a given sound.

**Overtones:** the term overtone is used for the frequencies HIGHER than the fundamental that are ACTUALLY PRESENT in the given sound. The first frequency higher than the fundamental is the first overtone, the next higher one is the second overtone, and so on.

**The distinction:** harmonics are the possible integral multiples of the fundamental; overtones are the ones actually produced, counted in ascending order. So the numbering need not agree:

| system | frequencies present | overtone numbering |
|---|---|---|
| string, or pipe open at both ends | \( n, 2n, 3n, 4n, \ldots \) (all harmonics) | 1st overtone \( = 2n \) (2nd harmonic) |
| pipe closed at one end | \( n, 3n, 5n, 7n, \ldots \) (odd harmonics only) | 1st overtone \( = 3n \) (3rd harmonic) |

Thus in a pipe closed at one end the even harmonics are missing, and the \( p \)-th overtone is the \( (2p+1) \)-th harmonic.

For a string of length \( l \) fixed at BOTH ends, a node forms at each end.

**Fundamental (first harmonic):** the string vibrates in one loop, so
\( l = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \qquad \therefore \lambda = 2l \qquad \therefore n = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{v}{2l} \)

**Second harmonic:** the string vibrates in two loops, so
\( l = \lambda_1 \qquad \therefore \lambda_1 = l \qquad \therefore n_1 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{v}{l} \)

The speed \( v \) is the same in both cases (same string, same tension), so
\( \dfrac{n}{n_1} = \dfrac{v/2l}{v/l} = \dfrac{1}{2} \)

\( \therefore \) the ratio of the fundamental frequency to the second harmonic is \( 1 : 2 \).

Given: \( y = 0.2 \sin 4\pi\left[ \dfrac{t}{0.08} - \dfrac{x}{0.8} \right] \) in SI units.

Expand the bracket to bring it to the standard form \( y = A\sin(\omega t - kx) \):

\( y = 0.2 \sin\left( \dfrac{4\pi}{0.08}t - \dfrac{4\pi}{0.8}x \right) = 0.2 \sin(50\pi t - 5\pi x) \)

Comparing with \( y = A\sin(\omega t - kx) \):
\( A = 0.2 \) m, \( \omega = 50\pi\ \mathrm{rad\ s}^{-1} \), \( k = 5\pi\ \mathrm{rad\ m}^{-1} \).

**(a) Wavelength**
\( \lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} = \dfrac{2\pi}{5\pi} = 0.4 \) m

**(b) Frequency**
\( n = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{50\pi}{2\pi} = 25 \) Hz

**(c) Amplitude**
\( A = 0.2 \) m

\( \therefore \) wavelength \( = 0.4 \) m, frequency \( = 25 \) Hz, amplitude \( = 0.2 \) m.

(As a check, the wave speed is \( v = n\lambda = 25 \times 0.4 = 10\ \mathrm{m\ s}^{-1} \), which also equals \( \dfrac{\omega}{k} = \dfrac{50\pi}{5\pi} \).)

A progressive (travelling) wave is one in which the disturbance produced in the medium travels continuously in a given direction, without damping or obstruction, from one particle to the next.

**Characteristics of progressive waves:**

1. Each particle of the medium executes the same type of vibration; the particles perform simple harmonic motion about their mean positions.
2. All vibrating particles of the medium have the SAME amplitude, period and frequency.
3. The PHASE (the state of vibration of a particle) changes continuously from one particle to the next.
4. No particle remains permanently at rest. Each particle comes to rest only momentarily, at the extreme positions of its vibration.
5. The particles attain their maximum velocity while passing through their mean positions.
6. Energy is transferred along the direction of propagation of the wave; there is NO transfer of matter.
7. The wave propagates through the medium with a definite velocity, which depends upon the properties of the medium.
8. Progressive waves are of two types — transverse and longitudinal.
9. In a transverse wave the particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation, producing crests and troughs; in a longitudinal wave they vibrate along the direction of propagation, producing compressions and rarefactions.
10. Both transverse and longitudinal mechanical waves can travel through solids, but only longitudinal waves can travel through fluids.

A stationary (standing) wave is produced by the superposition of two identical progressive waves travelling through the same medium along the same path in OPPOSITE directions.

**Characteristics of stationary waves:**

1. They are produced by the superposition of two identical waves (transverse or longitudinal) travelling in opposite directions along the same path.
2. Some points of the medium remain permanently at rest; these are called NODES. Points that oscillate with the greatest amplitude are called ANTINODES. Points in between vibrate with amplitudes lying between \( 0 \) and the maximum.
3. Two identical transverse waves give a transverse stationary wave; two identical longitudinal waves give a longitudinal stationary wave.
4. The distance between two consecutive nodes is \( \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \), and the distance between two consecutive antinodes is also \( \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \).
5. Nodes and antinodes are produced alternately; the distance between a node and the adjacent antinode is \( \dfrac{\lambda}{4} \).
6. The amplitude of vibration varies periodically with position, but ALL points vibrate with the same frequency.
7. Although every particle except those at the nodes possesses energy, there is NO propagation of energy. The wave is localised and its velocity is zero — which is why it is called a stationary wave.
8. All the particles between two adjacent nodes (i.e. within one loop) vibrate IN PHASE. There is no progressive change of phase from particle to particle; the phase simply reverses in the adjacent loop.

All particles also cross their mean positions simultaneously, which does not happen in a progressive wave.

Consider two identical simple harmonic progressive waves of amplitude \( a \), frequency \( n \) and wavelength \( \lambda \), travelling along a stretched string in OPPOSITE directions — one being the incident wave and the other the wave reflected from the far end.

The wave travelling along the \( +x \) direction is
\( y_1 = a\sin\left\{ 2\pi\left( nt - \dfrac{x}{\lambda} \right) \right\} \)

and the wave travelling along the \( -x \) direction is
\( y_2 = a\sin\left\{ 2\pi\left( nt + \dfrac{x}{\lambda} \right) \right\} \)

By the PRINCIPLE OF SUPERPOSITION the resultant displacement is
\( y = y_1 + y_2 = a\sin\left\{ 2\pi\left( nt - \dfrac{x}{\lambda} \right) \right\} + a\sin\left\{ 2\pi\left( nt + \dfrac{x}{\lambda} \right) \right\} \)

Using \( \sin C + \sin D = 2\sin\left( \dfrac{C+D}{2} \right)\cos\left( \dfrac{C-D}{2} \right) \), with
\( \dfrac{C+D}{2} = 2\pi nt \) and \( \dfrac{C-D}{2} = -\dfrac{2\pi x}{\lambda} \), and since \( \cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta \):

\( y = 2a\sin(2\pi nt)\cos\dfrac{2\pi x}{\lambda} \)

or \( y = 2a\cos\dfrac{2\pi x}{\lambda}\sin(2\pi nt) \)

Writing \( A = 2a\cos\dfrac{2\pi x}{\lambda} \), this becomes
\( y = A\sin(2\pi nt) = A\sin\omega t \qquad (\omega = 2\pi n) \)

This is the equation of a stationary wave on a stretched string. The terms in position \( x \) and time \( t \) appear as SEPARATE factors, so the waveform does not advance — unlike a progressive wave, where \( x \) and \( t \) occur together in a single phase.

**Nodes:** the amplitude \( A \) is zero when \( \cos\dfrac{2\pi x}{\lambda} = 0 \), i.e. at
\( x = \dfrac{\lambda}{4},\ \dfrac{3\lambda}{4},\ \dfrac{5\lambda}{4},\ \ldots \) — successive nodes being \( \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \) apart.

**Antinodes:** the amplitude is maximum, \( |A| = 2a \), when \( \cos\dfrac{2\pi x}{\lambda} = \pm 1 \), i.e. at
\( x = 0,\ \dfrac{\lambda}{2},\ \lambda,\ \dfrac{3\lambda}{2},\ \ldots \) — successive antinodes also \( \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \) apart, and each midway between two nodes.

The two waves have the same frequency, amplitudes \( A_1 \) and \( A_2 \), and differ in phase by \( \varphi \):
\( y_1 = A_1\sin\omega t \qquad y_2 = A_2\sin(\omega t + \varphi) \)

By the principle of superposition the resultant displacement is
\( y = y_1 + y_2 = A_1\sin\omega t + A_2\sin(\omega t + \varphi) \)

Expanding \( \sin(\omega t + \varphi) \):
\( y = A_1\sin\omega t + A_2\sin\omega t\cos\varphi + A_2\cos\omega t\sin\varphi \)

Collecting the \( \sin\omega t \) and \( \cos\omega t \) terms:
\( y = \left( A_1 + A_2\cos\varphi \right)\sin\omega t + \left( A_2\sin\varphi \right)\cos\omega t \)

Put
\( A_1 + A_2\cos\varphi = A\cos\theta \qquad \ldots (1) \)
\( A_2\sin\varphi = A\sin\theta \qquad \ldots (2) \)

Then \( y = A\cos\theta\sin\omega t + A\sin\theta\cos\omega t = A\sin(\omega t + \theta) \), so the resultant is again a simple harmonic wave of the same frequency, with amplitude \( A \) and phase constant \( \theta \).

Squaring and adding (1) and (2):
\( A^2\cos^2\theta + A^2\sin^2\theta = \left( A_1 + A_2\cos\varphi \right)^2 + \left( A_2\sin\varphi \right)^2 \)

\( A^2 = A_1^2 + 2A_1A_2\cos\varphi + A_2^2\cos^2\varphi + A_2^2\sin^2\varphi \)

Using \( \cos^2\varphi + \sin^2\varphi = 1 \):
\( A^2 = A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1A_2\cos\varphi \)

\( \therefore A = \sqrt{ A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1A_2\cos\varphi } \)

**Special cases:**

| phase difference \( \varphi \) | \( \cos\varphi \) | resultant amplitude |
|---|---|---|
| \( 0,\ 2\pi,\ 4\pi,\ \ldots \) (in phase) | \( +1 \) | \( A = A_1 + A_2 \) — maximum, constructive interference |
| \( \pi,\ 3\pi,\ \ldots \) (out of phase) | \( -1 \) | \( A = |A_1 - A_2| \) — minimum, destructive interference |

Dividing (2) by (1) also gives the phase of the resultant, \( \tan\theta = \dfrac{A_2\sin\varphi}{A_1 + A_2\cos\varphi} \).

The fundamental frequency of a stretched string of vibrating length \( l \), under tension \( T \), of linear density (mass per unit length) \( m \), is
\( n = \dfrac{1}{2l}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{m}} \)

Three laws follow from this formula.

**1) Law of length:** the fundamental frequency of vibration of a string is inversely proportional to the length of the vibrating string, if the tension and the mass per unit length are constant.
\( n \propto \dfrac{1}{l} \), if \( T \) and \( m \) are constant.

**2) Law of tension:** the fundamental frequency of vibration of a string is directly proportional to the square root of the tension, if the vibrating length and the mass per unit length are constant.
\( n \propto \sqrt{T} \), if \( l \) and \( m \) are constant.

**3) Law of linear density:** the fundamental frequency of vibration of a string is inversely proportional to the square root of the mass per unit length, if the tension and the vibrating length are constant.
\( n \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}} \), if \( T \) and \( l \) are constant.

**Verification using a sonometer**

A sonometer is a hollow rectangular wooden sound box carrying a uniform metal wire fixed at one end and passing over a pulley at the other, from which a hanger with slotted weights is suspended so that the tension can be varied. Two movable bridges P and Q allow the vibrating length to be changed.

In each experiment a light PAPER RIDER is placed on the wire midway between the bridges. A tuning fork is set into vibration and its stem is held against the sonometer box. The bridges are moved until the wire vibrates with maximum amplitude and the paper rider is thrown off — that is the length at which the wire is in RESONANCE with the fork, so the frequency of the wire equals the known frequency of the fork.

**(i) First law:** keeping the tension \( T \) constant, a set of tuning forks of known frequencies \( n_1, n_2, n_3, \ldots \) is used and the corresponding resonating lengths \( l_1, l_2, l_3, \ldots \) are noted. It is found that
\( n_1l_1 = n_2l_2 = n_3l_3 = \ldots = \) constant
\( \therefore n \propto \dfrac{1}{l} \) — the first law is verified.

**(ii) Second law:** keeping the vibrating length \( l \) and the wire (hence \( m \)) constant, the tension is changed so that the same length resonates with forks of different frequencies. If tensions \( T_1, T_2, T_3, \ldots \) correspond to frequencies \( n_1, n_2, n_3, \ldots \), it is found that
\( \dfrac{n_1}{\sqrt{T_1}} = \dfrac{n_2}{\sqrt{T_2}} = \dfrac{n_3}{\sqrt{T_3}} = \ldots = \) constant
\( \therefore n \propto \sqrt{T} \) — the second law is verified.

**(iii) Third law:** two wires of different linear densities \( m_1 \) and \( m_2 \) are used. Under the SAME tension, each is made to resonate with the same tuning fork, and the resonating lengths \( l_1 \) and \( l_2 \) are noted. It is found that
\( l_1\sqrt{m_1} = l_2\sqrt{m_2} = \) constant
But by the first law \( n \propto \dfrac{1}{l} \), and here \( n \) is the same for both wires, so
\( \therefore n \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}} \) — the third law is verified.

In this way all three laws of a vibrating string are verified using a sonometer.

Consider a cylindrical pipe of length \( l \) closed at one end, containing an air column. At the CLOSED end the air particles have least freedom to move, so a NODE must form there. Just beyond the OPEN end the particles are most free, so an ANTINODE forms there. Taking \( e \) as the end correction, the corrected length of the air column is \( L = l + e \).

Let \( v \) be the speed of sound in air.

**Fundamental mode (first harmonic).** One node at the closed end and one antinode at the open end, with no node or antinode between them:
\( L = \dfrac{\lambda}{4} \qquad \therefore \lambda = 4L \)
\( \therefore n = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{v}{4L} = \dfrac{v}{4(l+e)} \)

**First overtone.** The air column now contains one extra node and one extra antinode:
\( L = \dfrac{3\lambda_1}{4} \qquad \therefore \lambda_1 = \dfrac{4L}{3} \)
\( \therefore n_1 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{3v}{4L} = 3\left( \dfrac{v}{4L} \right) \)
\( \therefore n_1 = 3n \) — the THIRD harmonic.

**Second overtone.** Two extra nodes and two extra antinodes:
\( L = \dfrac{5\lambda_2}{4} \qquad \therefore \lambda_2 = \dfrac{4L}{5} \)
\( \therefore n_2 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_2} = \dfrac{5v}{4L} = 5\left( \dfrac{v}{4L} \right) \)
\( \therefore n_2 = 5n \) — the FIFTH harmonic.

**Generalising.** Because a node is fixed at one end and an antinode at the other, the length of the air column must always be an ODD number of quarter wavelengths:
\( L = (2p+1)\dfrac{\lambda_p}{4} \), \( p = 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots \)
\( \therefore n_p = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_p} = (2p+1)\dfrac{v}{4L} \)
\( \therefore n_p = (2p+1)\,n \)

Since \( (2p+1) \) is always ODD, the frequencies present are \( n, 3n, 5n, 7n, \ldots \)

\( \therefore \) only the ODD harmonics are present in the vibrations of an air column in a pipe closed at one end; the even harmonics \( 2n, 4n, 6n, \ldots \) are absent.

The reason is the boundary condition itself: an even harmonic would require an even number of quarter wavelengths in the column, which would place the SAME kind of point (node or antinode) at both ends — impossible when one end is closed and the other open.

Consider a cylindrical pipe of length \( l \) open at BOTH ends. At each open end the air particles have maximum freedom to vibrate, so an ANTINODE forms at (just beyond) each end. With \( e \) the end correction at each end, the corrected length of the air column is \( L = l + 2e \).

Let \( v \) be the speed of sound in air.

**Fundamental mode (first harmonic).** Antinodes at the two ends with one node between them:
\( L = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \qquad \therefore \lambda = 2L \)
\( \therefore n = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{v}{2L} = \dfrac{v}{2(l+2e)} \)

**First overtone.** Three antinodes and two nodes are formed:
\( L = \lambda_1 \qquad \therefore \lambda_1 = L \)
\( \therefore n_1 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{v}{L} = 2\left( \dfrac{v}{2L} \right) \)
\( \therefore n_1 = 2n \) — the SECOND harmonic.

**Second overtone.** Four antinodes and three nodes are formed:
\( L = \dfrac{3\lambda_2}{2} \qquad \therefore \lambda_2 = \dfrac{2L}{3} \)
\( \therefore n_2 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_2} = \dfrac{3v}{2L} = 3\left( \dfrac{v}{2L} \right) \)
\( \therefore n_2 = 3n \) — the THIRD harmonic.

**Generalising.** Since an antinode is required at each end, the length of the air column must be a whole number of HALF wavelengths:
\( L = (p+1)\dfrac{\lambda_p}{2} \), \( p = 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots \)
\( \therefore n_p = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_p} = (p+1)\dfrac{v}{2L} \)
\( \therefore n_p = (p+1)\,n \)

As \( p \) takes the values \( 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots \), the factor \( (p+1) \) takes EVERY positive integer value, so the frequencies present are \( n, 2n, 3n, 4n, 5n, \ldots \)

\( \therefore \) ALL harmonics are present as overtones in the vibrations of an air column in a pipe open at both ends.

(Contrast the pipe closed at one end, where the unlike boundary conditions at the two ends permit only the odd harmonics.)

Given: frequency \( n = 500 \) Hz, speed \( v = 350 \) m/s.

**(a) Phase difference at one point, between instants \( 1.0 \) ms apart**

At a FIXED point the phase advances only with time, at the rate \( \omega = 2\pi n \). Hence
\( \Delta\phi = \omega\,\Delta t = 2\pi n\,\Delta t \)
\( \Delta\phi = 2\pi \times 500 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-3} = \pi\ \mathrm{rad} \)

\( \therefore \) the phase difference is \( \pi \) radian \( = 180^\circ \). (Equivalently, \( 1.0 \) ms is exactly half the period \( T = \dfrac{1}{500} = 2.0 \) ms.)

**(b) Smallest distance between two points \( 45^\circ \) out of phase at one instant**

At a FIXED instant the phase changes only with position, a separation of one full wavelength corresponding to \( 360^\circ \). First find the wavelength:
\( \lambda = \dfrac{v}{n} = \dfrac{350}{500} = 0.7 \) m

Then
\( \Delta x = \left( \dfrac{\Delta\phi}{360^\circ} \right)\lambda = \dfrac{45}{360} \times 0.7 = \dfrac{0.7}{8} = 0.0875\ \mathrm{m} \)

\( \therefore \) the smallest distance is \( 0.0875 \) m \( = 8.75 \) cm.

\( \therefore \) (a) \( \pi \) rad, (b) \( 8.75 \) cm.

Given: distance between two successive nodes \( = 3.75 \) cm \( = 3.75 \times 10^{-2} \) m, speed of sound \( v = 1500 \) m/s.

In a stationary wave the distance between two successive nodes is \( \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \).

\( \therefore \dfrac{\lambda}{2} = 3.75 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m} \)
\( \therefore \lambda = 7.5 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m} = 0.075\ \mathrm{m} \)

The stationary wave has the same wavelength and frequency as the progressive waves that produced it, so
\( n = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1500}{0.075} = 20\,000\ \mathrm{Hz} \)

\( \therefore \) the frequency is \( 2 \times 10^{4} \) Hz \( = 20 \) kHz.

(This lies just at the upper limit of the audible range.)

Given: separation of the sources \( d = 4 \) m, frequency \( n = 330 \) Hz, speed \( v = 330 \) m/s, and the two sources are \( 180^\circ \) (i.e. \( \pi \) rad) OUT OF PHASE.

Wavelength:
\( \lambda = \dfrac{v}{n} = \dfrac{330}{330} = 1\ \mathrm{m} \)

**Condition for maximum intensity.** At a point where the path difference is \( \Delta \), the total phase difference between the two arriving waves is the phase difference of the SOURCES plus that due to the path:
\( \Delta\phi = \pi + \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta \)

The intensity is maximum when \( \Delta\phi = 2q\pi \) with \( q \) an integer:
\( \pi + \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta = 2q\pi \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta = (2q-1)\pi \)
\( \therefore \Delta = (2q-1)\dfrac{\lambda}{2} \)

So for ANTIPHASE sources the maxima occur where the path difference is an ODD multiple of \( \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \) — exactly the reverse of the in-phase case.

With \( \lambda = 1 \) m, \( \dfrac{\lambda}{2} = 0.5 \) m, so
\( \Delta = 0.5,\ 1.5,\ 2.5,\ 3.5\ \mathrm{m},\ \ldots \)

**Locating the points.** Take the mid-point of the two sources as origin, so the sources are at \( -2 \) m and \( +2 \) m. For a point at a distance \( x \) from the centre, LYING BETWEEN the sources, the two path lengths are \( (x+2) \) and \( (2-x) \), so
\( \Delta = (x+2) - (2-x) = 2x \)

\( \therefore 2x = 0.5,\ 1.5,\ 2.5,\ 3.5 \)
\( \therefore x = 0.25,\ 0.75,\ 1.25,\ 1.75\ \mathrm{m} \)

The next value, \( \Delta = 4.5 \) m, would give \( x = 2.25 \) m, which lies outside the region between the sources and is rejected. By symmetry the same values occur on the other side of the centre.

\( \therefore \) the intensity is maximum at \( \pm 0.25 \) m, \( \pm 0.75 \) m, \( \pm 1.25 \) m and \( \pm 1.75 \) m from the mid-point of the two sources — eight points in all. Note that the CENTRE itself (\( \Delta = 0 \)) is a point of MINIMUM intensity, because the sources are out of phase.

Given: speed \( v = 330 \) m/s, frequency \( n = 540 \) Hz (identical for both waves), distances from the two sources \( 3.5 \) m and \( 3 \) m, sources IN PHASE.

Wavelength:
\( \lambda = \dfrac{v}{n} = \dfrac{330}{540} = 0.6111\ \mathrm{m} \)

Path difference:
\( \Delta = 3.5 - 3 = 0.5\ \mathrm{m} \)

Since the sources are in phase, the whole phase difference comes from the path difference:
\( \Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta = \dfrac{2\pi \times 0.5}{0.6111} \)

It is neater to substitute \( \lambda = \dfrac{330}{540} \) directly:
\( \Delta\phi = 2\pi \times 0.5 \times \dfrac{540}{330} = \pi \times \dfrac{540}{330} = \dfrac{18}{11}\pi \)

\( \therefore \Delta\phi = 1.636\,\pi\ \mathrm{rad} \)

\( \therefore \) the phase difference between the waves is \( 1.636\,\pi \) radian \( \approx 294.5^\circ \) \( ( \approx 5.14\ \mathrm{rad}) \).

As this is neither an even nor an odd multiple of \( \pi \), the point is neither a point of maximum nor of minimum intensity.

Given: \( T_1 = 1.5 \) kg wt, \( T_2 = 6 \) kg wt, \( l_1 = 60 \) cm, and the two wires have the SAME fundamental frequency, \( n_1 = n_2 \).

Both wires are of the same material and the same cross section, so they have the same linear density \( m \).

The fundamental frequency of a stretched wire is
\( n = \dfrac{1}{2l}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{m}} \)

Since \( n_1 = n_2 \),
\( \dfrac{1}{2l_1}\sqrt{\dfrac{T_1}{m}} = \dfrac{1}{2l_2}\sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{m}} \)

The factors \( 2 \) and \( \sqrt{m} \) cancel, leaving
\( \dfrac{l_2}{l_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}} \)

The tensions are the weights of the loads, and their common factor \( g \) cancels inside the ratio, so the loads in kilograms may be used directly:
\( \dfrac{l_2}{l_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{6}{1.5}} = \sqrt{4} = 2 \)

\( \therefore l_2 = 2\,l_1 = 2 \times 60 = 120\ \mathrm{cm} \)

\( \therefore \) the vibrating length of the other wire is \( 120 \) cm \( = 1.2 \) m.

(The more heavily loaded wire must be LONGER, since a greater tension by itself would raise the frequency.)

Given: a pipe closed at one end produces overtones at \( 640 \) Hz, \( 896 \) Hz and \( 1152 \) Hz.

For a pipe closed at one end only ODD harmonics are present, so if the fundamental is \( n \) the frequencies available are
\( n,\ 3n,\ 5n,\ 7n,\ 9n,\ \ldots \)

The three given frequencies are CONSECUTIVE overtones, so they are consecutive odd multiples of \( n \). Any two consecutive odd multiples differ by \( 2n \):

\( 896 - 640 = 256\ \mathrm{Hz} \)
\( 1152 - 896 = 256\ \mathrm{Hz} \)

The two differences agree, which confirms that the frequencies are consecutive terms of the series.

\( \therefore 2n = 256 \)
\( \therefore n = 128\ \mathrm{Hz} \)

**Check.** With \( n = 128 \) Hz:
\( \dfrac{640}{128} = 5 \), \( \dfrac{896}{128} = 7 \), \( \dfrac{1152}{128} = 9 \)

All three are odd multiples, as a closed pipe requires. They are the fifth, seventh and ninth harmonics, i.e. the SECOND, THIRD and FOURTH overtones.

\( \therefore \) the fundamental frequency is \( 128 \) Hz.

Given: fundamental frequency \( n = 300 \) Hz, speed of sound \( v = 340\ \mathrm{m\ s}^{-1} \), tube OPEN at both ends.

For a pipe open at both ends an antinode forms at each end, so in the fundamental mode the air column holds half a wavelength:
\( L = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \qquad \therefore \lambda = 2L \)

\( \therefore n = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{v}{2L} \)

\( \therefore L = \dfrac{v}{2n} = \dfrac{340}{2 \times 300} = \dfrac{340}{600} \)

\( \therefore L = 0.5667\ \mathrm{m} \)

\( \therefore \) the length of the tube in the fundamental mode is about \( 0.5666 \) m \( \approx 56.7 \) cm.

(The end correction has been neglected here; including it, this \( L \) would be the corrected length \( l + 2e \), so the actual pipe would be slightly shorter.)

Given: length \( L = 25 \) cm \( = 0.25 \) m, speed of sound \( v = 330 \) m/s, pipe OPEN at both ends.

**Fundamental frequency (first harmonic).** An antinode at each open end gives \( L = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \), so \( \lambda = 2L = 0.5 \) m.
\( n = \dfrac{v}{2L} = \dfrac{330}{2 \times 0.25} = \dfrac{330}{0.5} = 660\ \mathrm{Hz} \)

**First overtone.** In a pipe open at both ends ALL harmonics are present, so the first overtone is the SECOND harmonic:
\( n_1 = 2n = 2 \times 660 = 1320\ \mathrm{Hz} \)

**Second overtone.** This is the THIRD harmonic:
\( n_2 = 3n = 3 \times 660 = 1980\ \mathrm{Hz} \)

\( \therefore \) the fundamental, first overtone and second overtone frequencies are \( 660 \) Hz, \( 1320 \) Hz and \( 1980 \) Hz respectively.

(Had the pipe been closed at one end, the first and second overtones would instead have been \( 3n \) and \( 5n \), since the even harmonics would be missing.)

Given: fundamental frequency of the OPEN pipe \( n_{o} = 600 \) Hz, speed of sound \( v = 330 \) m/s. The first overtone of the CLOSED pipe equals the first overtone of the open pipe.

**Length of the open pipe.** An antinode forms at each open end, so \( L_{o} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \) and
\( n_{o} = \dfrac{v}{2L_{o}} \)
\( \therefore L_{o} = \dfrac{v}{2n_{o}} = \dfrac{330}{2 \times 600} = \dfrac{330}{1200} = 0.275\ \mathrm{m} \)
\( \therefore L_{o} = 27.5\ \mathrm{cm} \)

**First overtone of the open pipe.** All harmonics are present in an open pipe, so its first overtone is the second harmonic:
\( n_{o,1} = 2n_{o} = 2 \times 600 = 1200\ \mathrm{Hz} \)

**Length of the closed pipe.** Only odd harmonics are present in a pipe closed at one end, so ITS first overtone is the THIRD harmonic — this is the step the question is really testing:
\( n_{c,1} = \dfrac{3v}{4L_{c}} \)

Setting this equal to \( 1200 \) Hz:
\( 1200 = \dfrac{3 \times 330}{4L_{c}} \)
\( \therefore L_{c} = \dfrac{3 \times 330}{4 \times 1200} = \dfrac{990}{4800} = 0.20625\ \mathrm{m} \)
\( \therefore L_{c} = 20.625\ \mathrm{cm} \)

\( \therefore \) the open pipe is \( 27.5 \) cm long and the closed pipe is \( 20.625 \) cm long.

Given: length of string \( L = 1 \) m, frequency of the imposed vibrations \( n = 15 \) Hz, and the stationary wave contains FOUR complete loops. The string is fixed at one end and its other end is free.

**Setting up the mode.** The fixed end must be a NODE. As the hint states, the free end is an ANTINODE. Each complete loop (the portion between two successive nodes) is \( \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \) long, and the final stretch from the last node out to the free antinode is a further \( \dfrac{\lambda}{4} \).

So with four complete loops plus that terminal quarter,
\( L = 4 \times \dfrac{\lambda}{2} + \dfrac{\lambda}{4} = 2\lambda + \dfrac{\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{9\lambda}{4} \)

(Equivalently, a fixed-free string satisfies \( L = (2p-1)\dfrac{\lambda}{4} \); four complete loops corresponds to \( p = 5 \), giving \( L = \dfrac{9\lambda}{4} \).)

**Wavelength.**
\( \dfrac{9\lambda}{4} = 1\ \mathrm{m} \)
\( \therefore \lambda = \dfrac{4}{9} = 0.4444\ \mathrm{m} \)

**Speed of the progressive wave.**
\( v = n\lambda = 15 \times \dfrac{4}{9} = \dfrac{60}{9} = 6.667\ \mathrm{m\ s}^{-1} \)

\( \therefore \) the speed of the progressive wave is \( 6.67\ \mathrm{m\ s}^{-1} \).

Note how much the free end matters: had BOTH ends been nodes, four loops would give \( L = 2\lambda \), hence \( \lambda = 0.5 \) m and \( v = 7.5\ \mathrm{m\ s}^{-1} \) — a different answer. The terminal quarter wavelength at the free antinode is exactly what the hint is pointing at.

Given: fundamental frequency of the violin string \( n = 440 \) Hz.

A violin string is fixed at BOTH ends, so a node forms at each end and ALL harmonics are present:
\( n_p = p\,n \), \( p = 1, 2, 3, \ldots \)

**First overtone** is therefore the SECOND harmonic:
\( n_1 = 2n = 2 \times 440 = 880\ \mathrm{Hz} \)

**Second overtone** is the THIRD harmonic:
\( n_2 = 3n = 3 \times 440 = 1320\ \mathrm{Hz} \)

\( \therefore \) the first and second overtones are \( 880 \) Hz and \( 1320 \) Hz respectively.

(Keep the two numberings apart: the \( p \)-th overtone of a stretched string is the \( (p+1) \)-th harmonic.)

Given: 8 tuning forks in increasing order of frequency; each fork gives \( 4 \) beats per second with the NEXT one; the last fork has twice the frequency of the first.

Let the frequency of the first fork be \( n_1 \).

Since each fork gives 4 beats per second with the next, and the frequencies increase, each successive frequency is \( 4 \) Hz greater than the one before it. The frequencies form an arithmetic progression with common difference \( 4 \) Hz:
\( n_p = n_1 + (p-1) \times 4 \)

For the eighth (last) fork, \( p = 8 \):
\( n_8 = n_1 + (8-1) \times 4 = n_1 + 28 \)

But it is given that the last fork has twice the frequency of the first:
\( n_8 = 2n_1 \)

Equating the two expressions:
\( 2n_1 = n_1 + 28 \)
\( \therefore n_1 = 28\ \mathrm{Hz} \)
\( \therefore n_8 = 2 \times 28 = 56\ \mathrm{Hz} \)

\( \therefore \) the frequency of the first fork is \( 28 \) Hz and that of the last fork is \( 56 \) Hz.

(Check: the series runs \( 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48, 52, 56 \) Hz — eight forks, each \( 4 \) Hz above the previous, and \( 56 = 2 \times 28 \).)

Given: initial tension \( T_1 = 40 \) N, at which the wire is in UNISON with a fork of frequency \( n_1 = 384 \) Hz; the tension is then decreased by \( 1.24 \) N.

Being in unison means the wire's frequency equals the fork's, so \( n_1 = 384 \) Hz.

New tension:
\( T_2 = 40 - 1.24 = 38.76\ \mathrm{N} \)

The vibrating length and the linear density are unchanged, so by the law of tension \( n \propto \sqrt{T} \):
\( \dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}} \)

\( \therefore n_2 = 384 \times \sqrt{\dfrac{38.76}{40}} = 384 \times \sqrt{0.969} = 384 \times 0.98438 \)

\( \therefore n_2 = 378\ \mathrm{Hz} \)

The frequency has DECREASED, as it must when the tension is reduced.

**Beat frequency** (number of beats per second) is the difference of the two frequencies:
\( \Delta n = n_1 - n_2 = 384 - 378 = 6\ \mathrm{Hz} \)

The question asks for the number of beats in TWO seconds:
\( \text{beats in 2 s} = 6 \times 2 = 12 \)

\( \therefore 12 \) beats are produced in two seconds.

Given: vibrating length \( l = 0.5 \) m, stretching weight \( = 5 \) kg, fundamental frequency \( n = 100 \) Hz.

The tension is the weight of the load:
\( T = 5 \times 9.8 = 49\ \mathrm{N} \)

The fundamental frequency of a stretched wire is
\( n = \dfrac{1}{2l}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{m}} \)

where \( m \) is the linear density (mass per unit length). Rearranging for \( m \):
\( 2ln = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{m}} \)
\( \therefore (2ln)^2 = \dfrac{T}{m} \)
\( \therefore m = \dfrac{T}{(2ln)^2} \)

Substituting:
\( m = \dfrac{49}{(2 \times 0.5 \times 100)^2} = \dfrac{49}{(100)^2} = \dfrac{49}{10\,000} \)

\( \therefore m = 4.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg/m} \)

\( \therefore \) the linear density of the wire is \( 4.9 \times 10^{-3} \) kg/m (i.e. \( 4.9 \) g per metre).

Given: full length of the string \( l_1 = 80 \) cm, its fundamental frequency \( n_1 = 112 \) Hz; required frequency \( n_2 = 160 \) Hz.

Pressing the string at a point shortens the VIBRATING LENGTH; the tension and the linear density are unchanged. So by the law of length,
\( n \propto \dfrac{1}{l} \qquad \therefore n_1 l_1 = n_2 l_2 \)

\( \therefore l_2 = \dfrac{n_1 l_1}{n_2} = \dfrac{112 \times 80}{160} \)

\( \therefore l_2 = \dfrac{8960}{160} = 56\ \mathrm{cm} \)

The required frequency is HIGHER than the fundamental, so the vibrating length must be SHORTER than \( 80 \) cm — and \( 56 \) cm duly is.

\( \therefore \) the guitarist should press the string at a point \( 56 \) cm from one end (that is, \( 80 - 56 = 24 \) cm from the other end), leaving \( 56 \) cm free to vibrate.
